batchName: Middle Republic: Scipio and the Road to Zama (216-201 BCE) - Hard Batch 1
chapterName: Middle Republic: Scipio and the Road to Zama (216-201 BCE)

questions.question: What finally broke the deadlock between the Roman infantry and Hannibal's veteran third line at Zama?
options: Fleeing elephants trampled the Carthaginian line
Roman cavalry returned and struck the Carthaginian rear
Reinforcements arrived from the siege of Utica
Hannibal's veterans ran out of javelins
Scipio's reserve line outflanked the veterans
Masinissa's infantry broke through the centre
questions.explanation: The two sides fought "with the greatest fire and fury" until the Roman cavalry came back and hit the enemy from behind. Polybius counted 20,000 Carthaginians killed against 1,500 Roman dead.
questions.sourceQuote: Neither gave way until the Roman cavalry returned and struck the Carthaginian rear.

questions.question: Which of the following contributed to the Carthaginian disaster at the Metaurus in 207 BC? (select all that apply)
options: Hannibal sent troops to block his retreat
Masinissa's horsemen attacked his rear
Claudius Nero struck his flank with half his men
His weary army was trapped beside a river
His guides deserted him during the night retreat
His elephants were sent down lanes by trumpets
questions.explanation: Deserted by his guides and trapped at the river, Hannibal's brother was then hit in the flank by Claudius Nero. The trumpets and lanes belong to Zama, and Masinissa was not at the Metaurus.
questions.sourceQuote: In the battle, Claudius Nero led half his men behind the Roman lines and smashed into the enemy flank.

questions.question: How do modern historians view the story that after Cannae Scipio forced young nobles plotting to flee abroad to swear loyalty at sword-point?
options: They think it happened after Zama instead
They suspect it was invented
They think the nobles meant to join Hannibal
They accept it as confirmed by Polybius
They place the episode at the Ticinus
They credit the deed to Scipio's father
questions.explanation: The tale of Scipio bursting in on the would-be deserters is a later story that modern historians doubt. What is clear is that he survived Cannae and rallied the stragglers.
questions.sourceQuote: Modern historians suspect it was invented.

questions.question: What restriction did the Senate's compromise place on Scipio's recruitment for the African expedition?
options: He could take no more than a single legion
He could use only allied, non-Roman troops
He could recruit only from Sicilian cities
He could not sail until Hannibal left Italy
He had to share command with the princeps senatus
He could not call up soldiers normally, only ask for volunteers
questions.explanation: Scipio was limited to volunteers rather than a normal levy. He drilled his army for about a year, from units of 80 men up to the whole force.
questions.sourceQuote: But he could not call up soldiers in the usual way, only ask for volunteers.

questions.question: According to Polybius, why did Scipio order his men to kill everyone they met when New Carthage fell?
options: To avenge his father and uncle
To punish a massacre of Roman refugees
To stop the garrison escaping by sea
To terrify the region into surrender
To honour Neptune with a sacrifice
Because his soldiers had mutinied
questions.explanation: Polybius saw the slaughter as deliberate terror, claiming soldiers even cut dogs in half. Once the citadel surrendered, Scipio spared the citizens and enslaved only non-citizens.
questions.sourceQuote: Polybius, a Greek historian of the period, thought the aim was to terrify the region into surrender, and claimed the soldiers even cut dogs in half.

questions.question: Which city, modern Cádiz, was Carthage's last stronghold in Spain, giving up soon after Ilipa?
options: Baecula
Utica
Gades
Italica
New Carthage
Ilipa
questions.explanation: Gades surrendered after Scipio's decisive victory at Ilipa. The mopping-up before it was harsh, and the people of one town killed themselves rather than surrender.
questions.sourceQuote: Soon Gades, modern Cádiz, Carthage's last stronghold in Spain, gave up too.

questions.question: What did Carthage do after Hannibal returned from Italy with his veterans?
options: Surrendered Utica to Scipio as a gesture
Asked Masinissa to mediate a peace
Accepted Scipio's terms without a fight
Sent Hannibal on to reconquer Spain
Executed the generals beaten at the Great Plains
Rejected a draft treaty Rome's Senate had approved
questions.explanation: Hannibal's return restored Carthage's nerve, so it rejected the draft treaty. He had landed with 15,000 to 20,000 veterans but few horses.
questions.sourceQuote: His arrival restored Carthage's nerve, and it rejected a draft treaty that Rome's Senate had already approved.

questions.question: Roughly how many reinforcements did Scipio bring with him when he arrived in Spain in 210 BC?
options: About 7,000
About 40,000
About 25,000
About 10,000
About 15,000
About 4,000
questions.explanation: Scipio reached Spain in early autumn with about 10,000 reinforcements. He was taking over after his father and uncle had been killed there.
questions.sourceQuote: Scipio arrived in Spain in early autumn with about 10,000 reinforcements.

questions.question: Which of these were terms of the peace Carthage accepted in 201 BC? (select all that apply)
options: It could fight in Africa only with Rome's permission
It could keep only ten warships
It could not wage war outside Africa at all
It had to tear down its city walls
It had to hand over Spain to Masinissa
It had to surrender Hannibal to Rome
questions.explanation: Carthage lost the right to make war freely and was cut down to ten warships. Masinissa's Numidian kingdom was also confirmed.
questions.sourceQuote: It could not wage war outside Africa at all, nor inside Africa without Rome's permission.

questions.question: Against the legend of divine visions, what did Polybius argue lay behind Scipio's success?
options: Careful planning and clear thinking
Genuine favour from the god Neptune
Steady backing from the Senate
Masinissa's superior cavalry
Sheer luck on the battlefield
The devotion of his Spanish allies
questions.explanation: Polybius rejected the tales of gods and prophetic dreams and credited Scipio's own planning and judgment. Some legends even had Spaniards hailing Scipio as king and god.
questions.sourceQuote: Polybius disagreed, arguing that Scipio succeeded through careful planning and clear thinking.
